stated.value: Relatively clear whey stream and opaque milk concentrate
Protein and fat, where relevant, referenced to laboratory results
Compare different measurement interfaces before choosing the installation
First measurement concepts and a comparison experiment for both streams

missing: Whey type and composition range (sweet or acid whey, protein level, whether fat is measured at all in whey)
Concentrate total solids, protein and fat range, and fat globule or particle size
Process temperature range, pressure, flow rate and whether flow is continuous or batch
Pipe diameter, available tapping points, and whether a bypass loop is possible
Hygienic requirements (3-A or EHEDG, CIP/SIP, steam exposure, product contact materials)

status_reason: The two streams are physically very different (clear low-solids whey versus strongly scattering concentrate), so a first measurement concept can be proposed, but process conditions, lab reference quality and target accuracy are not yet defined, so the choice of installation cannot be final.
answer: Use near-infrared (NIR) spectroscopy as the main technique for both streams, but with different optical interfaces: a short-path transmission cell or flow cell on the clear whey, and a diffuse-reflectance or transflectance probe on the opaque concentrate. Run a paired, lab-referenced comparison of these interfaces on each stream before choosing the installation, and treat fat in whey as a low-priority or possibly unmeasurable target.

inline.headline: Two optical interfaces on one NIR platform: short-path transmission for whey, reflectance or transflectance probe for concentrate, both calibrated against lab data before any installation decision
inline.method: NIR spectroscopy (about 900-2500 nm, with the water combination band near 1940 nm and the protein and fat CH/NH bands near 1700-1750 nm and 2300-2350 nm), with separate calibrations per stream. Transmission for whey, diffuse reflectance or transflectance for concentrate. Spectra should be taken at a controlled product temperature.
inline.probe: Whey: a sanitary flow cell with a short, fixed optical path (typically 1-5 mm, to be chosen in testing) and sapphire windows, mounted in a bypass or sidestream. Concentrate: a sanitary reflectance or transflectance probe with a sapphire window and a defined sample gap, sized so that light is returned from a thin surface layer. Probes should be cleanable in place and shaped to avoid air pockets and fat or protein deposits.
inline.install: Pilot as a sidestream or bypass loop with a pump and temperature control, so flow and temperature can be held constant during measurement. Install the whey cell and the concentrate probe on separate points or as a comparison bench, so that the two interfaces do not influence each other. Put a bubble trap or degassing step before the concentrate probe. Locate the sensor where the sample is representative and well mixed, and place the lab sampling point as close to it as possible.
inline.fiber: Low-OH silica fiber suited to NIR, with a core of about 400-600 µm, kept as short as the layout allows, since fiber length adds loss and temperature sensitivity. Use sealed, sanitary-rated connectors and fiber protection against heat and CIP chemicals. If Raman is tested later, use a low-fluorescence fiber and check background contribution.
inline.test_against: Laboratory protein by a validated reference method (for example Kjeldahl or Dumas nitrogen with a protein factor, per ISO 8968-1) and fat by a validated gravimetric method (for example Rose-Gottlieb per ISO 1211, or Gerber as a routine check). Use paired samples taken at the sensor point at the same time as the spectra, with the same sample handling for both streams.
inline.not_final_because: The best interface depends on the measured transmission or reflectance of the actual streams at real process temperature and solids, on the achievable calibration accuracy against the lab method, and on hygiene and installation constraints that are not yet known. Fat in whey may be too low to measure with useful precision, which would change the scope for that stream.

problems.text: Transmission through the milk concentrate at a normal flow cell path length will not work: the opaque, strongly scattering matrix gives almost no transmitted signal. Concentrate needs reflectance or transflectance geometry, or a very short path if transmission is retained.

One calibration cannot be assumed to serve both streams. Whey and concentrate differ in protein and fat levels, total solids, scattering and temperature, so separate models, or at least separate validation, are needed for each stream.

Fat in whey may not be a meaningful target. Whey is usually low in fat, and fat results at that level will have a large relative lab error, so fat measurement in whey may be below the detection limit or not worth the effort. This should be confirmed with the customer.

Protein in clear whey is at a low concentration compared with concentrate. NIR precision at low protein levels is limited, so the achievable accuracy on whey should be checked against the required tolerance before assuming it is met.

Lab reference quality and timing: protein and fat lab results have their own repeatability and sampling delay. If the lab sample is not taken at the same point and moment as the spectrum, the calibration error will include sampling error, which can exceed the sensor error.

Process temperature and air bubbles: temperature changes shift water and protein bands, and entrained air or gas bubbles in the concentrate strongly change the reflectance signal. Both must be controlled or measured and included in the calibration.

Fouling and cleaning: fat and protein films on the window will change the signal over time and may be aggravated by CIP. The cleaning cycle, window material and drift control must be planned before a long-term installation.

methods.method: NIR transmission in a short-path flow cell
methods.why: Suited to the clear whey stream, where enough light passes through a thin, well-defined path to give a good signal for protein and, if present, fat. Short path length avoids saturation of the water bands.

methods.method: NIR diffuse reflectance or transflectance probe
methods.why: Needed for the opaque concentrate, where transmission is not possible. Light is returned from a thin surface layer, so the result depends on sample gap, scattering and surface condition, which must be controlled.

Gives chemical information with little interference from water and can be less affected by scattering. It is worth comparing for protein and fat, but fluorescence from milk components and the cost of the probe need to be tested before it is chosen.

Highly specific for fat and protein and widely used for milk. Its very short penetration depth makes it sensitive to fouling and to sample contact, and it is less suited to a flow installation unless fouling is solved, so it is kept as a backup.
Could add sensitivity for low whey protein through aromatic amino acid signals. It is an option only if NIR precision on whey is insufficient, because it is sensitive to matrix and sample conditions.
Not a composition method, but a supporting measurement that can provide a scattering or particle covariate for correcting concentrate spectra, especially if globule size or solids vary.
Can measure fat and water content, but it is expensive and sensitive to temperature and flow conditions, and it does not directly give protein, so it is not a practical inline option for this pilot.

questions.q: What are the protein and fat levels and their ranges in the whey, and is fat actually a target for the whey stream?
questions.why: Determines whether fat is measurable in whey and whether the whey cell needs a long or short path.

questions.q: What are the total solids, protein and fat ranges in the concentrate, and what is the typical fat globule or particle size?
questions.why: Drives the reflectance geometry, sample gap and the expected scattering level.

questions.q: What are the process temperature range, pressure, flow rate and flow pattern (continuous or batch)?
questions.why: Temperature and flow affect the spectra and the sample presentation, and must be controlled or included in the calibration.

questions.q: Which laboratory methods are used for protein and fat, what is their repeatability, and how are samples taken and timed?
questions.why: Lab error sets the lower limit on achievable calibration accuracy, and mismatched sampling is a common cause of poor models.

questions.q: How many paired lab samples per stream can be collected over the pilot, and over what period and range of compositions?
questions.why: Sets the calibration and validation sample size and whether the models can cover the process range.

questions.q: What accuracy or tolerance is required for protein and fat, and what control or reporting action depends on it?
questions.why: Defines the go or no-go criterion and the acceptable measurement uncertainty.

questions.q: Are there hygienic requirements (3-A, EHEDG, CIP/SIP, steam exposure, product-contact materials) and is the area hazardous?
questions.why: Determines the probe and cell design, window materials, and whether certified equipment is needed.

questions.q: What pipe sizes and tapping points are available, and is a bypass or sidestream loop possible?
questions.why: Determines whether the cell or probe can be installed in the main line or only in a bypass.

questions.q: What is the maximum distance between the process and the spectrometer, and what fiber routing is possible?
questions.why: Fiber length drives signal loss and temperature sensitivity and may decide whether the spectrometer can sit close to the process.

experiment.objective: Compare two NIR optical interfaces (short-path transmission cell and diffuse reflectance or transflectance probe) on the whey and concentrate streams, against laboratory protein and fat results, to decide the measurement interface and the achievable accuracy for each stream before any permanent installation.
steps: Agree the lab reference methods, sampling point, and sample handling with the customer, and confirm the sampling point is the same as the sensor point.

Set up a bypass or sidestream loop with temperature control, and install a short-path transmission cell (for whey) and a reflectance or transflectance probe (for concentrate) on separate, well-defined points.
Collect a baseline of spectra at 2-3 controlled product temperatures and check the effect of entrained air using a degassing step on the concentrate.

Collect paired spectra and lab samples over the full expected composition range for each stream, aiming for at least 40-60 samples per stream, spread across several days and batches to capture real variation.
Test the path length (whey) and sample gap (concentrate) in a short range-finding set to choose the best geometry before the main calibration.
Build PLS calibration models per stream and per interface using a calibration set, and evaluate them on an independent validation set, using cross-validation during development.
Check whether fat in whey can be modelled at all; if the lab values are near the detection limit, report this instead of forcing a model.
Compare interfaces on RMSECV or RMSEP, bias, and RPD for each variable, and check the effect of temperature, bubbles and window fouling on the prediction error.
If NIR precision on whey is insufficient, run a short second test with Raman or fluorescence on the whey stream only, to see whether it adds information.
Write a short summary of the best interface and expected accuracy per stream, and the requirements for the installation (cleaning, temperature control, fiber routing).
references: ISO 8968-1: Milk and milk products - Determination of nitrogen content (Kjeldahl principle), for protein reference
ISO 1211: Milk - Determination of fat content (gravimetric method, Rose-Gottlieb)
ISO 9622 (IDF 141): Milk and liquid milk products - Guidelines for the application of mid-infrared spectrometry, for calibration and validation practice
Workman, J. and Weyer, L., Practical Guide to Interpretive Near-Infrared Spectroscopy (CRC Press, 2007), for NIR calibration and validation
Burns, D.A. and Ciurczak, E.W. (eds.), Handbook of Near-Infrared Analysis (CRC Press), for NIR sampling geometry and reflectance or transmission choice
experiment.go_no_go: Go for an installation concept for a stream if, on the independent validation set, the prediction error for protein and fat (where fat is a target) is within the agreed tolerance and the RPD is at a level the customer accepts (commonly above about 3 for process control), with stable performance across temperature and bubble tests and a cleaning cycle that does not cause unacceptable drift. No-go or re-scope if whey protein or any fat target cannot reach the tolerance, in which case the stream is re-scoped to a lab-first or at-line method.

multispectral.combination: Primary NIR on both streams, with a different optical interface per stream (transmission for whey, reflectance or transflectance for concentrate), plus a turbidity or light-scattering sensor as a covariate on the concentrate. Raman or fluorescence to be tested on whey only if NIR precision on low whey protein is insufficient.
multispectral.why: NIR responds to protein and fat through overtone and combination bands, and to water, which is the most common driver of error. The opaque concentrate scatters strongly, so a scattering covariate can correct for changes in globule size and solids. Whey has low protein and possibly no useful fat, where NIR may lack precision, so a second, more chemically specific technique is worth testing there.

assumptions: Both streams are milk-derived with a similar base matrix (water, lactose, protein, fat, minerals), so one NIR platform and one calibration approach are reasonable starting points.
Lab reference methods are validated and can be run on paired samples at the sensor point.
Process temperature stays within a range where the spectra can be corrected or controlled, and flow can be held or measured.
Fiber-optic NIR probes and cells are available for sanitary use at process temperature and pressure, with CIP-compatible materials.
No hazardous-area certification is needed for the pilot, unless the site classification says otherwise.
Fat in whey is assumed to be of low interest and may not be measurable, to be confirmed with the customer.

The pilot can run for several weeks with sampling across the normal production range, and the results are valid for the installation decision only if the process conditions in the pilot are representative.
